chapters.title: Chapter 2: Cyclical, Defensive, and Growth Sectors

lessons.title: Cyclical vs Defensive Sectors: How Earnings React to the Economy

body.text: People keep buying toothpaste in a recession. They postpone buying a car, a flat, or a new factory. That one difference in customer behaviour explains why some sectors' profits collapse when the economy slows while others barely notice, and it should shape what you expect from every stock you own.

children.text: Chapter 1 showed that sectors play by different rules. This chapter sorts them by the most important rule of all: how their earnings respond to the economic cycle. Get this classification right and you will stop being surprised when a 'great company' reports a terrible year, or when a 'boring' stock quietly holds up while the market falls.
The Core Difference: Can the Customer Wait?

markDefs.definition: Spending customers can postpone or cancel without immediate hardship, such as cars, holidays, homes, or new machinery. Its opposite is essential or non-discretionary spending.

children.text: Ask one question about any business: when money gets tight, can its customer delay the purchase? If yes, the business is cyclical. Its revenue depends on

by households, or on investment decisions by companies and governments, and both shrink quickly in a slowdown. If no, the business is defensive. Demand for medicines, basic food, soap, electricity, and mobile data stays relatively stable whether GDP is growing at 8% or contracting.

body.title: Cyclical vs Defensive at a Glance

columns.label: Cyclical sectors
points: Demand rises and falls with GDP growth, interest rates, and business confidence
Examples: autos, metals, cement, capital goods, real estate, hotels, airlines
Profits can multiply in a boom and shrink sharply or turn into losses in a downturn
Stocks usually fall harder than the Nifty in sell-offs and rise faster in recoveries

columns.label: Defensive sectors
points: Demand stays relatively steady through the cycle
Examples: FMCG staples, pharma, regulated power utilities, telecom
Profits grow slowly and steadily, with fewer sharp drops
Stocks usually fall less than the Nifty in sell-offs but often lag in strong rallies

children.text: It Is a Spectrum, Not Two Boxes

Real sectors sit somewhere along a line. Banks are cyclical through the credit cycle, but a large private bank with a strong deposit base behaves very differently from a steel company. FMCG is defensive, but premium products and urban discretionary categories slow down when household budgets tighten. Use this table as a starting map, then refine it company by company.

body.caption: Cyclicality Spectrum of Major Indian Sectors

cells: Global commodity prices and Chinese demand, on top of the domestic cycle
Interest rates, home loan affordability, and buyer confidence
Government and private capex; orders dry up when companies stop expanding
Consumer confidence, loan rates, fuel prices, and rural income
Loan growth slows and bad loans rise in downturns
Linked to the US and European economic cycle more than India's
Mobile data is now close to essential spending
Regulated returns and steady electricity demand
Medicine demand is stable; its risks are regulatory, not economic
Daily essentials; slowdowns hurt premium products and volumes only modestly

body.title: Which Is the Most Defensive?
body.question: India's GDP growth is forecast to slow sharply next year. Based purely on how each company's demand responds to the economy, which company's earnings are likely to hold up best?
body.explanation: Nestle India sells packaged food like Maggi noodles and milk products, which households keep buying in a slowdown. Maruti Suzuki sells cars, a purchase buyers can postpone. DLF sells real estate, which is highly sensitive to rates and confidence. Hindalco is a metals company exposed to global aluminium and copper prices.

children.text: What a Full Cycle Looks Like in the Earnings

The chart below tracks profits of two illustrative companies through one complete economic cycle, both starting at an index value of 100. The cement company's earnings more than double from trough to recovery but fall by more than half in between. The FMCG company's earnings hardly dip at all. Over the full six years, they end at almost the same place. The journey is what differs, and the journey is what drives the stock price and your nerves.

body.title: Illustrative Earnings Through One Economic Cycle (Year 1 = 100)
Measure the Peak-to-Trough Fall
body.prompt: Using the chart, the cement company's earnings peak at 125 in Year 2 and bottom at 45 in Year 4. By what percentage do its earnings fall from peak to trough? Enter the size of the fall as a positive number.
body.explanation: Fall = (125 - 45) ÷ 125 = 80 ÷ 125 = 64%. Compare the FMCG company: its peak of 115 dips to 112, a fall of only (115 - 112) ÷ 115, about 2.6%. That gap in earnings stability is exactly why the market prices these two businesses so differently.

children.text: A Real Stress Test: The 2020 Lockdown

The nationwide lockdown in 2020 was the most extreme test of this framework India has seen. It shut down discretionary spending almost overnight while essential spending continued. Watch how differently sectors experienced the same months.

body.title: How the 2020 Lockdown Sorted Cyclicals From Defensives

events.title: Nationwide lockdown announced
events.description: Factories, construction sites, showrooms, malls, and flights shut down. Only essential goods and services were allowed to operate.

events.title: Car sales fall to zero
events.description: Maruti Suzuki, India's largest carmaker, reported zero domestic sales for the month as dealerships stayed closed. Cement despatches and steel demand also collapsed with construction halted.

events.title: Essentials keep moving
events.description: Staples like atta, soap, and packaged food, along with medicines and mobile data, kept selling. Pharma and FMCG companies faced supply disruptions but not a demand collapse.

events.title: GDP data confirms the damage
events.description: Official data showed India's GDP for April to June 2020 contracted by nearly 24% year on year, the sharpest fall on record.

events.title: Cyclicals rebound hardest
events.description: As the economy reopened and interest rates stayed low, pent-up demand drove a sharp recovery in autos, metals, and real estate, whose earnings and stock prices bounced far more than defensives.

body.text: Defensive describes earnings, not stock prices. A defensive stock bought at a very high valuation can still fall sharply if growth disappoints or the market stops paying a premium for safety. Stable earnings protect you from an earnings collapse, not from overpaying.

body.title: A Portfolio Built for One Kind of Weather
body.scenario: Vikram built his portfolio during a strong economic upswing. He holds a two-wheeler maker, a cement company, a real estate developer, and a steel company, all bought after a year of rising profits. The RBI has now started raising interest rates to control inflation, and economists are cutting India's GDP growth forecasts.
body.prompt: What risk does Vikram's portfolio carry right now, and what questions should he ask before doing anything?
body.modelAnswer: All four holdings are cyclical, and three of them (two-wheelers, cement, real estate) are directly sensitive to interest rates and consumer confidence. Rising rates and slowing growth are exactly the conditions under which their earnings can fall together, so his portfolio is effectively one concentrated bet on the economy staying strong. He should ask: Has the market already priced in the slowdown, since cyclical stocks often fall before earnings do? How much debt does each company carry, since leveraged cyclicals suffer most in a downturn? How much would his portfolio fall if all four dropped together, and can he live with that? Would adding defensive sectors like FMCG or pharma reduce the swing? The goal is not to predict the cycle, but to avoid a portfolio that only works in one kind of economy.

body.title: Where do growth sectors fit in?

children.text: Cyclical vs defensive describes how earnings react to the economy. Growth describes how fast earnings expand over many years. They are two separate questions. A company can be defensive and growing, like a consumer business entering new categories. It can be cyclical and growing, like a capital goods firm riding a long infrastructure buildout. Growth stocks are often priced on earnings far in the future, which makes their prices especially sensitive to interest rates even if their demand is not. Keep both labels in mind: what happens to profits in a slowdown, and how fast profits compound over a decade.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: A sector is called ___ when its revenue and profits rise and fall sharply along with the economic cycle.
body.explanation: Cyclical sectors like autos, metals, cement, and real estate depend on spending that customers can postpone, so their earnings swing with the economy.

body.title: Test Any Company's Cyclicality on Screener.in
steps: Open the company page and scroll to the annual Profit & Loss table, which covers roughly the last decade
Check the year ending March 2021, which captures the lockdown impact, and see how far sales and net profit moved
Count how many years net profit fell compared to the previous year
Note the highest and lowest operating profit margin (OPM %) across the years; a wide range signals cyclicality
Compare the pattern with two or three sector peers to confirm it is an industry trait, not a company-specific problem
Label the company as cyclical, defensive, or in between, and write down the one factor that drives its swings

points: The key question is whether the customer can postpone the purchase; if yes, the sector is cyclical
Cyclical sectors such as metals, real estate, capital goods, autos, and cement see profits swing sharply with GDP growth, rates, and confidence
Defensive sectors such as FMCG staples, pharma, power utilities, and telecom have steadier earnings through the cycle
Cyclicality is a spectrum; banks, IT, and premium consumer products sit in between and must be judged company by company
The 2020 lockdown showed the framework in action: car sales went to zero while essentials kept selling, and cyclicals then rebounded hardest
Defensive means stable earnings, not a stock that cannot fall; overpaying for safety is still a risk
